Thailand Imposes Tariffs on Imported Power Transmission Equipment, Impacting Electric Utilities Industry

BANGKOK — The Electric Utilities industry in Thailand is experiencing significant changes following the government’s recent decision to impose a 25% tariff on imported power transmission equipment, including transformers, high-voltage cables, and switchgear. The new measure, which took effect last month, is intended to support domestic manufacturing but has already begun to affect operations at utilities firms and their employees across the country.

Officials from the Ministry of Commerce stated that the tariffs are designed to “encourage local production and ensure national energy security.” However, several Electric Utilities companies have reported delays in ongoing grid expansion projects and increased costs for maintaining existing infrastructure.

“We are facing immediate challenges sourcing essential components that are not produced locally at the required scale or quality,” said Narong Preecha, spokesperson for Siam National Electric, one of the country’s largest utilities. “This has led to project slowdowns and cost adjustments. Some scheduled upgrades to regional substations have been postponed until we can secure alternative supplies.”

Industry analysts estimate that, since the tariff was introduced, procurement costs for key equipment have risen by 18% on average. This has put pressure on utilities’ budgets, with some companies now reviewing operational plans and capital expenditures for the remainder of the year. “We have had to reassess our planned investments and re-negotiate contracts with our suppliers,” said a senior manager at Eastern Power Grid Co., who requested anonymity.

The impact is being felt at the local level as well. Workers at several sites under construction in Chonburi and Nakhon Ratchasima provinces reported reduced overtime hours and temporary reassignments as companies adjust their schedules. “We understand the policy’s intent but hope for support while the industry adapts,” said Sakda Limthong, a union representative at the Chonburi Transmission Project. “Some of our members are concerned about job stability if delays continue.”

The Electric Utilities Association of Thailand has urged the government to consider transitional support measures, such as temporary exemptions for critical imports and investment in domestic manufacturing capacity. “We believe the policy can benefit the country in the long run, but the transition period will be challenging for utilities and their staff,” said Chairwoman Kanchana Chatchawan.

As of this week, the industry continues to navigate the new trade environment, with several major transmission upgrades and maintenance projects currently under review. Government officials have indicated they will monitor the situation and hold consultations with industry representatives in the coming weeks.
